passages.text: The mutational repertoire of uterine sarcomas and carcinosarcomas in a Brazilian cohort: A preliminary study
OBJECTIVES:

The present study aimed to contribute to the catalog of genetic mutations involved in the carcinogenic processes of uterine sarcomas (USs) and carcinosarcomas (UCSs), which may assist in the accurate diagnosis of, and selection of treatment regimens for, these conditions.
METHODS:

We performed gene-targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) of 409 cancer-related genes in 15 US (7 uterine leiomyosarcoma [ULMS], 7 endometrial stromal sarcoma [ESS], 1 adenosarcoma [ADS]), 5 UCS, and 3 uterine leiomyoma (ULM) samples. <sentence_start/>Quality, frequency, and functional filters were applied to select putative somatic variants.
RESULTS:

Among the 23 samples evaluated in this study, 42 loss-of-function (LOF) mutations and 111 missense mutations were detected, with a total of 153 mutations. <sentence_start/>Among them, 66 mutations were observed in the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> (48%), <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (22%), and <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic> (17%) were the most frequently mutated genes. <sentence_start/>With respect to specific tumor subtypes, ESS showed mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">IGTA10</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">DST</italic> genes, UCS exhibited mutations in <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic>, and ULMS showed exclusive alterations in <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic>. <sentence_start/>Mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">KMT2A</italic> gene were observed exclusively in ULM and ULMS. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">In silico</italic> pathway analyses demonstrated that many genes mutated in ULMS and ESS have functions associated with the cellular response to hypoxia and cellular response to peptide hormone stimulus. <sentence_start/>In UCS and ADS, genes with most alterations have functions associated with phosphatidylinositol kinase activity and glycerophospholipid metabolic process.
CONCLUSION:

This preliminary study observed pathogenic mutations in US and UCS samples. <sentence_start/>Further studies with a larger cohort and functional analyses will foster the development of a precision medicine-based approach for the treatment of US and UCS.
INTRODUCTION

Sarcomas are rare heterogeneous tumors that affect the female genital tract and originate from tissues such as muscle, fat, bones, and fibrous tissue. <sentence_start/>Uterine sarcomas (USs) are the most commonly occurring gynecological sarcomas, representing 90% of the total cases (<citation rid="B01" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tjog.2016.04.033" pmid="27590365" count="1">1</citation>). <sentence_start/>Based on their histological composition, uterine tumors with mesenchymal elements can be divided into 1) pure sarcomas (uterine leiomyosarcomas - ULMSs, endometrial stromal sarcomas - ESSs); 2) mixed epithelial and mesenchymal tumors (adenosarcomas - ADSs), and 3) carcinosarcomas - UCSs, a biphasic tumor composed of high-grade carcinomatous and sarcomatous components derived from transdifferentiation of carcinoma (<citation rid="B02" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Many studies have characterized UCS tumors as mixed USs; however, since 2014, they have been reclassified as endometrial carcinomas (ECs) that demonstrate metaplastic features (<citation rid="B03" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers10090315" pmcid="PMC6162723" pmid="30200635" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B04" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ijgo.12613" pmid="30306577" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Despite their low prevalence, USs are associated with high rates of local recurrence, distant metastases, and poor prognosis, with two-year survival rates below 50% (<citation rid="B01" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tjog.2016.04.033" pmid="27590365" count="1">1</citation>).

Several genetic alterations have been associated with USs and UCSs, with few alterations being associated with specific histological subtypes. <sentence_start/>For instance, ESSs can be divided into two types: low-grade ESS (LG-ESS) and high-grade ESS (HG-ESS), both characterized by recurrent chromosomal translocations. <sentence_start/>In LG-ESS, the most common translocation, t [7; 17] (p15; q21), is observed in almost 50% of the cases and results in the <italic toggle="yes">JAZF1-SUZ12</italic> gene fusion (<citation rid="B05" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vaccines6030056" pmcid="PMC6161160" pmid="30149610" count="1">5</citation>). <sentence_start/>Ma et al. (<citation rid="B06" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.13270" pmid="27845897" pmcid="PMC5354813" count="1">6</citation>), revealed that the JAZF1-SUZ12 fusion protein destabilizes polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), abolishes histone methyltransferase (HMT) activity, and subsequently activates genes normally repressed by PRC2. <sentence_start/>JAZF1-PHF1, EPC1-PHF1, PHF1-MEAF6, MBTD1-CXorf67, and JAZF1-BCORL1 are other less frequent fusion proteins observed in the patients with these tumors. <sentence_start/>HG-ESS exhibits a <italic toggle="yes">YWHAE-NUTM2</italic> gene rearrangement (previously termed <italic toggle="yes">YWHAE-FAM22</italic>). <sentence_start/>Recently, molecular alterations in ZC3H7B-BCOR, BCOR-ITD, EPC1-BCOR, JAZF1-BCORL1, and BRD8-PHF1 have been identified. <sentence_start/>This histological subtype demonstrates more aggressive clinical behavior and worse prognosis (<citation rid="B05" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/vaccines6030056" pmcid="PMC6161160" pmid="30149610" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B02" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Many previous studies have investigated the ESS genome with a focus on genetic fusions (<citation rid="B07" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13023-016-0400-8" pmid="26879382" pmcid="PMC4754953" count="1">7</citation>-<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ijc.28440" pmid="23959973" count="1">10</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, Choi et al. (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.5384" pmid="26429873" pmcid="PMC4741768" count="1">11</citation>) demonstrated that fusions are not the only genetic alterations that occur during the development of ESS. <sentence_start/>Using whole-exome sequencing methods, the aforementioned study described mutations in <italic toggle="yes">PTEN</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">CDH1</italic>. <sentence_start/>Despite the use of a very small number of ESS samples in this study (3 LG-ESS), it is a valuable contribution to the understanding of the pathogenesis of such tumors.

ULMSs are not characterized by specific chromosome translocations; however, they are associated with a complex karyotype with chromosomal gains and losses, such as deletion in chromosome 1. <sentence_start/>Most ULMSs express PDGFR-α, WT1, CYP19, and GNRH-R (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(09)70226-8" pmid="19959075" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejrad.2010.12.057" pmid="21247711" count="1">13</citation>). <sentence_start/>Owing to gene alterations, the loss of function in the tumor suppressor genes, <italic toggle="yes">BRCA1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MED12</italic> as well as the loss of expression of the proteasome β1i subunit LMP2 have been associated with ULMS development (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/mco.2013.124" pmid="24649216" pmcid="PMC3916197" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Research Network (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2017.10.014" pmid="29100075" pmcid="PMC5693358" count="1">15</citation>) examined the molecular characterization of adult soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) and observed that ULMSs shared more similarities with extrauterine LMSs than that with other sarcomas. <sentence_start/>Although both tumors exhibit the same pattern of cell differentiation, their tumor environments are extremely diverse. <sentence_start/>This study included 53 cases of soft-tissue LMS (extrauterine) and 27 ULMS cases that were evaluated by whole-exome sequencing, demonstrating frequent alterations in <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATRX</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MED12</italic> (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cas.13613" pmid="29660202" pmcid="PMC5989874" count="1">16</citation>).

Somatic mutations have also been described occurring at low frequency in the majority of the tyrosine kinase growth factor gene family and their targets, namely, v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1 (<italic toggle="yes">BRAF</italic>), <italic toggle="yes">CDKN2A</italic>, epidermal growth factor receptor (<italic toggle="yes">EGFR</italic>), <italic toggle="yes">HER2,</italic> v-kit Hardy-Zuckerman 4 feline sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (<italic toggle="yes">KIT</italic>), v-Ki-ras2 Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (<italic toggle="yes">KRAS</italic>), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (<italic toggle="yes">PDGFR</italic>), and phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase, catalytic subunit α (<italic toggle="yes">PI3KCA</italic>) during the development of UCS. <sentence_start/>In addition, mutations in <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PTEN</italic>, protein phosphatase 2 scaffold subunit alpha (<italic toggle="yes">PPP2R1A)</italic>, F-box, and WD repeat domain containing 7 (<italic toggle="yes">FBXW7</italic>) have already been identified, which may contribute to the development of therapeutic alternatives including the use of the inhibitors of PARP, EZH2, cell-cycle, and PI3K pathway (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/mco.2013.124" pmid="24649216" pmcid="PMC3916197" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2017.02.010" pmid="28292439" pmcid="PMC5599133" count="1">17</citation>). <sentence_start/>Little information is available on how mutations contribute to ADS etiology; however, one study observed that <italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic> mutations are associated with the tumorigenic process in a small subset of such tumors (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41379-018-0132-5" pmid="30266945" count="1">18</citation>).

Since these are rare tumors, only a few studies focusing on the definition of the mutational repertoire of the different histological types of rare sarcomas have been conducted thus far. <sentence_start/>Therefore, studies focusing on the mutational characterization of these tumors are of paramount importance and will contribute to the discovery of new biomarkers for precision medicine-based approaches in the treatment of such neoplasms. <sentence_start/>Herein, we investigated the mutational profile of the samples obtained from patients with ULMSs, UCSs, ESSs, and ADSs, using a commercial panel containing 409 cancer-associated genes involved in apoptosis, signaling, transcription regulation, inflammation response, and growth factors-associated pathway.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Sample selection

In order to analyze differences in genetic mutations between different histological types of US, we initially selected 43 formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) human samples including 14 ULMS, 12 ESS, 2 ADS, 12 UCS, and 3 ULM-non-cancerous tumor (as reference samples). <sentence_start/>All samples were obtained via surgical procedures performed between 2000 and 2012 at the Institute of Cancer of Sao Paulo (ICESP) and Clinics Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP). <sentence_start/>Tissues were stored at the molecular and structural gynecology laboratory (LIM-58) of the University of Sao Paulo Medical School (FMUSP).

This study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the FMUSP with protocol number 477/15. <sentence_start/>Patients' medical records were revised and the following data were recorded: age at diagnosis, postmenopausal bleeding, adjuvant treatment, presence of metastasis or recurrence, and status.
DNA Isolation

Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit obtained from QIAGEN<sup>®</sup> according to the manufacturer’s instructions. <sentence_start/>DNA concentration, purity, and integrity were assessed by spectrophotometry (Nanodrop 2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and fluorometry (Qubit - Thermo Fisher Scientific), respectively.
Preparation of sequencing libraries and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)

Sequencing libraries were prepared using the Ion Torrent Ampliseq Comprehensive Cancer Panel - Catalog number: 4477685 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), which contains ∼16,000 primer pairs multiplexed into 4 pools. <sentence_start/>This commercial panel was designed to assess the mutational profile of 409 cancer driver genes and drug targets along with signaling cascades, apoptosis genes, DNA repair genes, transcription regulators, inflammatory response genes, and growth factor genes (Table S1). <sentence_start/>Prior to amplification, DNA was treated with the uracil-DNA glycosylase enzyme (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by adding 1 unit of enzyme per 50 ng of DNA and incubating for 15 min at 37 °C. <sentence_start/>This procedure was performed to remove DNA molecules containing uracil and decrease the number of artifactual variants in the sequencing (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s41241-019-0075-2" count="1">19</citation>). <sentence_start/>Libraries were then prepared using Ion AmpliSeq<sup>TM</sup> Library kit 2.0 protocols, with 10 ng of input DNA per pool, totaling 40 ng of DNA from each sample. <sentence_start/>The FuPa reagent was used to partially digest primer sequences and phosphorylate the amplicons. <sentence_start/>Next, sequencing adaptors and barcodes were ligated to the amplicon by the enzyme Ligase using the Ion Xpress™ Barcode Adapters kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), which were then purified using magnetic beads (Agencourt<sup>®</sup> AMPure<sup>®</sup> XP Reagents, Beckman Coulter). <sentence_start/>Subsequently, emulsion PCR was performed using the Ion PI™ Hi-Q™ OT2 200 Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), followed by sequencing with Ion PI<sup>TM</sup> Hi-Q<sup>TM</sup> sequencing 200 and Ion PI<sup>TM</sup> Chip.
Data Analysis

The results were analyzed using the Torrent Suite v5.0.5 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). <sentence_start/>Sequence variants (SNVs and indels) were identified using the Torrent Variant Caller (Ion Torrent - Thermo Fisher Scientific) and compared to the GRCh37 / hg19 genome version. <sentence_start/>VCF files were analyzed using VarSeq v1.8 software (GoldenHelix) for variant annotation and prioritization. <sentence_start/>The variants were filtered based on the quality and frequency criteria: coverage (>100), genotype quality score cutoff (GQS>50), variant base in at least 5% of reads, variant base present in at least 2 reads in each direction, homopolymer-length error<5, absence of genetic variants in population databases (ExAC; NHLBI-ESP; 1000 Genomes Project) or minor allele frequency (MAF)≤0.01%.

Subsequently, variants were selected based on their effect on protein expression, with the following being considered: 1) variants described in the COSMIC database; 2) loss-of-function variants - Frameshift variants-nucleotide insertions/deletions, gain/loss of stop codons, splice site alterations); or 3) missense variants (in-frame insertions/deletions, amino acid exchange) predicted as possibly pathogenic in at least three of six prediction programs used (SIFT, PolyPhen, MutationTaster, MutationAssessor, FATHMM, FATHMM-MKL) and occurring in oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes in OncoMD database. <sentence_start/>Variants not previously described in the COSMIC database were visually inspected using the integrative genomics viewer (IGV) program to exclude sequencing artifacts.

Construction of genetic interaction networks was performed using Cytoscape platform version 3.7.0, which uses data from protein and genetic interactions, pathways, co-expression, co-localization, and protein domain similarity.
RESULTS

Initially, 40 US and UCS (14 ULMS, 12 ESS, 2 ADS, and 12 UCS) and 3 ULM samples were selected from the pathology department files; however, only 23 (7 ULMS, 7 ESS, 1 ADS, 5 UCS, and 3 ULM) remained until the end of NGS analyses. <sentence_start/>Some losses occurred while performing multiplex PCR reactions (AmpliSeq™), during which we observed a high degree of fragmented DNA and many genetic artifacts in several samples. <sentence_start/>These issues are expected since tissue processing for paraffin inclusion and long storage time causes damage to the DNA structure (integrity). <sentence_start/>The clinical and pathological features of 40 patients with US and UCS who were enrolled in this study are summarized in Table 1.

Among the 23 samples deemed suitable for the evaluation of sequencing data, homogeneity average was 73.2%, median base coverage was 1257X, and horizontal coverage was 84.3% corresponding to 100X. Based on the NGS data, we selected point mutations with possible impacts on the function of the protein encoded by the altered gene (missense, nonsense, splice-site mutations, loss of stop codons) and small insertions and deletions (indels). <sentence_start/>Total variants detected in each sample and filtered variants for the selection of somatic alterations of interest are presented in Table 2.

An average of 1700 alterations were identified per sample (ranging from 746 to 3521), with an average of 1606 single nucleotide variants (SNVs) (ranging from 678 to 3406), 40 insertions (ranging from 23 to 77), and 55 deletions (ranging from 25 to 114). <sentence_start/>To select relevant somatic variants, a first filter was applied focusing on the quality and frequencies of these alterations. <sentence_start/>A second filter, focusing on variant functions and effects, was used to select the alterations that would be most relevant in alterations of gene functions. <sentence_start/>Collectively, in 23 samples that were evaluated, 42 LOF mutations and 111 missense mutations were detected, with a total of 153 filtered mutations, among which 66 were found in the COSMIC database (Table 2).

Among the 409 genes included in the panel, mutations were detected in 94 distinct genes, with 30 genes demonstrating mutations in more than one sample and 64 genes showing mutations in a single sample. <sentence_start/>Table 3 presents the list of genes that were mutated in more than one sample of the cohort, along with the number of mutated samples and the histological types. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> (11/23 - 48%), <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (5/23 - 22%), and <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic> (4/23 - 17%) were the most frequently mutated genes.

The Venn diagram (Figure 1) shows the shared and individual (specific) mutations of each malignant histological subtype evaluated (ULMS, ESS, UCS, and ADS). <sentence_start/>Three shared genes were observed (<italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">KMT2D</italic>) among the ULMS, ESS, and UCS samples. <sentence_start/>Nineteen genes were shared between 2 types of tumors, and 68 genes were mutated in a single type. <sentence_start/>Among them, 6 genes were mutated in more than one sample of the same histological subtype, namely, <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic> (3 ESS samples), <italic toggle="yes">ITGA10</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">DST</italic> (2 ESS samples), <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic> (2 ULMS samples), and <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> (2 UCS samples). <sentence_start/>Quantitatively, this analysis shows similarities in the mutational profiles of ULMS and ESS, with 6 mutated genes in common (6.7%) between both subtypes. <sentence_start/>In the genes <italic toggle="yes">JAK3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATRX</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MYB</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">SYNE1</italic>, most of the mutations were characterized as missense mutations; however, in the <italic toggle="yes">SYNE1</italic> gene, the two mutations observed in ULMS and ESS samples were determined as LOF mutations (c.352C>T and c.8565G>A, respectively). <sentence_start/>In addition, mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">TRRAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">DNMT3A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">EPHA7</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">KAT6B</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">PRKDC</italic> genes indicate that UCS and ADS may exhibit molecular similarities.

Table 4 summarizes the genes with the most frequent alterations (mutations in 2 or more samples, or with 2 mutations in the same sample), the types of mutations, and their position. <sentence_start/>Alterations in the respective proteins are also indicated, along with the combined effect of these alterations (Missense or LOF) and DNA (c.), and protein (p.) nomenclatures. <sentence_start/>Their nomenclature can be used for database searches. <sentence_start/>The descriptions of the 153 potentially somatic variants are listed in Table S2. <sentence_start/>UCS5, ULMS52, , and ADS2 samples demonstrated the highest number of mutations (UCS5 with 20 mutations in 19 genes; ULMS52 with 11 mutations in 10 genes; with 10 mutations in 10 genes, and ADS2 with 16 mutations in 16 genes). <sentence_start/>Samples with the lowest number of mutations were ULMS50b with 1 mutation in ALK, ESS4 with 2 mutations (<italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic>), and ULM119 (benign tissue) with 2 mutations (<italic toggle="yes">MET</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PDGFB</italic>).

Based on the data described in Table 4, we selected genes with more than three mutations in our cohort to submit to the OncoPrinter visualization tool (cBioPortal - ). <sentence_start/>Figure 2 shows the percentage of patients demonstrating mutations in each gene, distribution, and the types of mutations observed in each sample. <sentence_start/>The highest frequency of gene mutations was observed in TP53 (48%) with the highest frequency of missense-type mutations (3 ULMS, 1 ESS, and 4 UCS samples). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> mutations were observed in 22% of the samples, with 3 missense-type mutations (2 ULMS and 1 ESS) and 2 LOF-type mutations (1 ESS and 1 UCS). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic> appeared to be the third most mutated gene (17%) present in 3 UCS samples, with most of the mutations determined as the missense-type. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MTOR</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TRRAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">KMT2D</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TSC2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">JAK3</italic> showed a 13% mutational frequency. <sentence_start/>LOF mutations in <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic> was found exclusively/specificaly in the ESS samples. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">NF1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MYB</italic> demonstrated a 9% mutational frequency. <sentence_start/>Missense mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MYB</italic> were associated with ULMS and ESS (4 mutations in ULMS and 2 in ESS).

Since uterine sarcomas are histologically classified into two primary subtypes, we used the same classification to study the association of the mutated genes with pure sarcomas (ULMS - ESS) and mixed tumors (UCS - ADS). <sentence_start/>Figure 3 shows the association of the mutated genes in the group of tumors classified as pure (ULMS and ESS). <sentence_start/>According to the Cytoscape platform (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.1239303" pmid="14597658" pmcid="PMC403769" count="1">20</citation>), many genes demonstrating mutations in these histological subtypes exhibit functions associated with the cellular response to hypoxia (<italic toggle="yes">MTOR</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PDK1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MDM2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CREBBP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH1,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HIF1A</italic>) and peptide hormone stimulus (<italic toggle="yes">EIF4EBP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RPTOR</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TSC2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TSC1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MTOR</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">JAK3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ADCY6</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">GNAS,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">ATP6V1D</italic>).

Although UCS is no longer classified as uterine sarcoma but as metaplastic carcinoma, we included this tumor group in the analysis shown in Figure 4. Here, we associated UCS - ADS owing to their mixed histologies (epithelial and mesenchymal components) and also because many retrospective studies on the US still include UCS in their available samples. <sentence_start/>According to the Cytoscape platform (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.1239303" pmid="14597658" pmcid="PMC403769" count="1">20</citation>), many mutated genes in these tumors have functions associated with phosphatidylinositol kinase activity (<italic toggle="yes">PI4K2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PI4KB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CG</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PI4KA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2G,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CD</italic>) and glycerophospholipid metabolic process (<italic toggle="yes">PI4K2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PI4KB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CG</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PI4KA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C3</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3C2G</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CD, PI4K2B,</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SMG1)</italic>.

Collectively, our results indicate that despite the molecular heterogeneity demonstrated by USs and UCSs, they share similarities in their mutational profiles. <sentence_start/>In addition, genetic interaction networks indicate that alterations in functions associated with hypoxia, response to peptide hormone stimulus in ULMSs and ESSs, and phosphatidylinositol kinase activity and glycerophospholipid metabolic process in UCS and ADS can influence the carcinogenic process of these tumors. <sentence_start/>Considering that NGS technology can provide a reliable molecular portrait of neoplasms quickly and cost-effectively (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30524974" pmcid="PMC6277731" count="1">21</citation>), these results open new avenues for research and consequently, may positively impact the clinical management of patients with such tumors.
DISCUSSION

In this study, we performed a mutational screening of the samples collected from patients with USs and UCSs. <sentence_start/>We employed a panel of 409 genes for the screening. <sentence_start/>Initially, we focused on the mutated genes shared among more than one histological subtype of US. <sentence_start/>We initiated our analyses with 40 samples, but owing to the quality of the FFPE material, certain losses reduced the number of samples to 23. <sentence_start/>Considering the published reports on sarcomas, the number of samples was sufficient for this type of population mutational screening. <sentence_start/>In UCS and ESS samples, we identified mutations in genes that demonstrated alterations in previous studies conducted for examining other tumors, such as <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">AR</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">NF</italic> (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2018.02.060" pmid="30096302" pmcid="PMC8045146" count="1">22</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although the role of these genes is known in different cancers, their role in the tumorigenesis of USs and USCs is not fully understood.

<italic toggle="yes">The PIK3CA</italic> gene encodes the p110α protein, the catalytic subunit of PI3K, which controls the growth, division, survival, movement, and structure of cells. <sentence_start/>Many studies have demonstrated the importance of <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic> mutation in mediating tumorigenesis via increased <italic toggle="yes">PI3K</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">AKT</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">mTOR</italic> signaling (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers12010093" pmcid="PMC7017171" pmid="31905960" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1096502" pmid="15016963" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>While investigating druggable molecular targets in uterine sarcomas, Cuppens et. al (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-16-2149" pmid="28232476" count="1">25</citation>) identified <italic toggle="yes">PI3K</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">MTOR</italic> as a potential target in 26% of cases, which were primarily ULMS, HG-ESS, and undifferentiated uterine sarcomas. <sentence_start/>Here, we included eight samples of ESS. <sentence_start/>Seven of these were characterized as HG-ESS, consistent with the molecular findings described in previous reports published for these tumors. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic> is critical for the regulation of expression of several miRNAs. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic> gene is highly conserved among various species, indicating that mutations may compromise its function and might be involved in the onset of tumors (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0811817106" pmid="19520829" pmcid="PMC2705554" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>Previous reports published by our group (<citation rid="B02" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms19010052" pmcid="PMC5796002" pmid="29295562" count="1">27</citation>) demonstrated the regulation of microRNAs associated with several oncogenic pathways, including <italic toggle="yes">DICER1.</italic> <sentence_start/>Mutations in <italic toggle="yes">NF1</italic> have already been demonstrated in soft-tissue sarcomas (myxofibrosarcomas and pleomorphic liposarcomas) (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bcp.2012.02.009" pmid="22387046" count="1">28</citation>). <sentence_start/>The expression of the androgen receptor (AR) seems to be associated with a better prognosis in patients with ESS. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">AR</italic> expression is higher in pre-malignant lesions and low-grade tumors (LG-ESS) (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/PGP.0000000000000353" pmid="28114189" count="1">29</citation>). <sentence_start/>These findings may explain why AR expression is low in ULMS, which is an extremely aggressive tumor (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3802/jgo.2018.29.e30" pmid="29533018" pmcid="PMC5920217" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the effects of the mutations observed in this gene need to be further investigated for US.

It is important to note that <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH1</italic> was the unique gene that shared mutations in the UCS and ULMS. <sentence_start/>Similarly, mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">DAXX</italic> gene have also been observed in the cases of ESS/ADS and ULMS/ADS, which share mutations in <italic toggle="yes">TSC2</italic>. <sentence_start/>Thus, our results suggest that besides exhibiting a similar tumor microenvironment, USs and UCSs also share genetic alterations. <sentence_start/>This observation is relevant to the understanding of the onset and evolution of these tumors. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, ULMS cases originating from ULMs have been reported; however, this hypothesis has not been proven yet (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jog.14037" pmid="31215132" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" count="1">32</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our study showed that mutations in <italic toggle="yes">KMT2A</italic> were exclusively observed in ULMS and ULM. <sentence_start/>The c.3019G>T variant appears to be related to the Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome and Kabuki syndrome (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41431-017-0023-0" pmid="29255178" pmcid="PMC5865196" count="1">34</citation>).

We attempted to identify specific genes for each type of tumor, establishing individual signatures. <sentence_start/>Despite the heterogeneity, we were able to identify six specific genes for three of the histological types evaluated in this study. <sentence_start/>In ESS samples, we observed variants in the <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic> (c.214C>T and c.2494delC), <italic toggle="yes">ITGA10</italic> (c.2104G>A), and <italic toggle="yes">DST (</italic>c.16429C>T) genes. <sentence_start/>The variant <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic> c.214C>T is described in the COSMIC database (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1">35</citation>) and was first observed in papillary thyroid carcinoma. <sentence_start/>Mutations in this gene are described in several tumors, such as breast cancer as well as the cancers of the endometrium, cervix, ovaries, and urinary tract. <sentence_start/>The protein encoded by the PDE4DIP gene is responsible for binding 4D phosphodiesterase to the Golgi complex. <sentence_start/>Alterations in this gene may cause a myeloproliferative disorder associated with eosinophilia (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00109-016-1395-2" pmid="26920370" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>Despite the information available in databases and the literature, its typical role in tumor biology remains unknown.

In UCS, we observed two variants of <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> (c.782A>C and c.2513G>A). <sentence_start/>The variant <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> c.2513G>A is described in the COSMIC database (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1">35</citation>) as pathogenic (score 0.99) and has already been observed in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, large bowel adenocarcinoma, malignant melanoma, and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. <sentence_start/>The role of <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> as a tumor progression factor is not fully elucidated. <sentence_start/>However, this gene is known to be overexpressed and/or mutated in several solid tumors (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ijc.21507" pmid="16187281" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>The monoclonal antibody <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> therapy is effective in breast, lung, and prostate cancer cells <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic> (<citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/fon.09.144" pmid="20021208" count="1">38</citation>). <sentence_start/>Specific and detailed studies may demonstrate new opportunities for the development of therapies targeting these tumors.

Mutations in <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic> have also been observed exclusively in ULMS. <sentence_start/>All variants are described in the COSMIC database (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>c.6094C>A mutation of <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> is considered to be pathogenic (score 0.97) and is described in diffuse large B cell lymphoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> c.7223T>A variant is also pathogenic (score 0.85) and has already been described in meningioma, a primary non-malignant CNS tumor (<citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/fon-2018-0006" pmid="30084265" pmcid="PMC6123887" count="1">39</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic> also presented two pathogenic variants in ULMS: c.236A>C and c.2446C>T. The c.236A>C variant has already been described in meningothelial meningioma and is associated with IL-6 signaling pathways and DNA damage response. <sentence_start/>The c.2446C>T mutation has been observed in large bowel adenocarcinoma and transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary system. <sentence_start/>Persistent <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> signaling is largely associated with poor clinical prognosis. <sentence_start/>In addition, it increases resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, making these cancers less sensitive to treatment (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31218097" pmcid="PMC6556604" count="1">40</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic> mutations have emerged as therapeutic targets for a variety of tumors. <sentence_start/>Anti- HER2 therapies are effective against breast, lung, and cervical cancers (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2019.03.010" pmid="30951733" pmcid="PMC6571037" count="1">41</citation>).

In this study, we were able to identify several mutations that contribute to a better understanding of the biology of USs and UCSs. <sentence_start/>Even with the limitations associated with rare tumors, we identified genetic alterations that might act as potential target markers for precision medicine-based approaches upon validation in larger cohorts. <sentence_start/>To date, there is no precise preoperative diagnostic test for these tumors. <sentence_start/>Although rare, such tumors are very aggressive and associated with a poor prognosis. <sentence_start/>Thus, even with small cohorts, the molecular profiling of USs and UCSs is extremely important to identify the changes driving the development of these tumors and provide powerful tools for diagnostic and prognostic tests as well as adequate treatment alternatives. <sentence_start/>Our study is the first DNA-sequencing study to investigate all histological types of USs and UCSs together and is an insightful contribution for defining the mutational repertoire of these rare tumors.
CONCLUSIONS

Using a platform to profile mutations in a panel of 409 genes, we identified that <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PIK3CA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">APC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MTOR</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">DICER1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TRRAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">KMT2D</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TSC2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">JAK3</italic> are the most frequently mutated genes in USs and UCSs. <sentence_start/>Considering common mutations among the different tumor types being evaluated, the <italic toggle="yes">TP53</italic> (4 UCS/4 ULMS/3 ESS), <italic toggle="yes">ATM</italic> (2 ULMS/2 ESS/1 UCS), and <italic toggle="yes">KMT2D</italic> (1 UCS/1 ULMS/1 ESS) genes could be indicators of similarities in neoplastic progression. <sentence_start/>As specific signature genes, ESS exhibited mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">PDE4DIP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">IGTA10</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">DST</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>UCS showed mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">ERBB4</italic> gene, and ULMS demonstrated exclusive alterations in the <italic toggle="yes">NOTCH2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HER2</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>Mutations in the <italic toggle="yes">KMT2A</italic> gene were observed exclusively in ULM and ULMS samples, and therefore, are potentially involved in the malignant transformation process. <sentence_start/>According to the Cytoscape platform, many genes that were mutated in the ULMS and ESS samples exhibit functions associated with the cellular response to hypoxia and peptide hormone stimulus. <sentence_start/>In UCS and ADS, most altered genes exhibit functions associated with phosphatidylinositol kinase activity and glycerophospholipid metabolic process. <sentence_start/>More studies should be conducted with a larger number of samples and functional analyses. <sentence_start/>However, the current screening contributes to the characterization of the complex genetic profile of USs and USCs.
